---
title: "11 — Annual mental distress and predictor distribution shifts"
output: html_notebook
---

**Measures:** annual survey-weighted frequent mental distress (2014–2025) and the distribution of each predictor during 2022–2025. This examines temporal changes that might affect generalization. It is *descriptive* and does not select or retrain models.

## Setup

Loads the unchanged input settings, shared model functions, and the persistent run increment. The output suffix identifies this run.

```{r setup}
# Set the project root, then load R code from the shared R Notebooks.
find_project_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
    current <- normalizePath(start, mustWork = TRUE)
    repeat {
        if (file.exists(file.path(current, "FMD_Project.Rproj"))) {
            return(current)
        }
        parent <- dirname(current)
        if (identical(parent, current)) {
            stop("Open FMD_Project.Rproj in RStudio first")
        }
        current <- parent
    }
}

project_root <- find_project_root()
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = project_root)

load_module <- function(name) {
    path <- file.path(project_root, "R", paste0(name, ".Rmd"))
    text <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
    starts <- which(startsWith(text, "```{r"))
    ends <- which(trimws(text) == "```")
    blocks <- lapply(starts, function(start) {
        finish <- ends[ends > start][1]
        if (is.na(finish) || finish <= start + 1L) {
            stop("Missing code or closing fence in ", path)
        }
        paste(text[(start + 1L):(finish - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
    })
    eval(parse(text = paste(blocks, collapse = "\n\n")), envir = parent.frame())
    invisible(TRUE)
}

load_module("config")
load_module("run_manager")
load_module("helpers")
load_module("plot_palette")
run_context <- attach_run()
cat("[RUN] Current increment:", run_context$id, "\n")
```



## Annual FMD trends

Compares reported FMD across years, showing patterns independently of model performance. The historical audit now contains additional confidence-interval and sample-size columns, while the 2025 checkpoint produces a simpler prevalence table. This notebook deliberately harmonizes the four comparable fields (`YEAR`, `cohort`, `observed_fmd`, and `n`) before combining years. The graph shows **point estimates only**; historical confidence intervals remain available in the annual audit output and should not be invented for 2025. The graph is printed in this notebook and saved with the increment suffix.

```{r annual-fmd-trend}
# Read existing annual historical estimates. The updated Audit notebook
# also saves standard errors, confidence intervals, and effective sample
# sizes, so we select only the fields needed for this 2014–2025 trend.
history_path <- artifact_path("tables", "01_annual_fmd_prevalence", "csv")
annual_history <- data.table::fread(history_path)

# Older audit runs may call the unweighted group count "respondents".
# Support both names without altering the source results.
if (!"n" %in% names(annual_history) && "respondents" %in% names(annual_history)) {
    data.table::setnames(annual_history, "respondents", "n")
}

required_columns <- c("YEAR", "cohort", "observed_fmd", "n")
missing_columns <- setdiff(required_columns, names(annual_history))
if (length(missing_columns) > 0L) {
    stop(
        "Historical annual prevalence table is missing: ",
        paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", ")
    )
}

annual_history <- annual_history[
    ,
    .(
        YEAR = as.integer(YEAR),
        cohort = as.character(cohort),
        observed_fmd = as.numeric(observed_fmd),
        n = as.integer(n)
    )
]

# The 2025 scored checkpoint retains the entire original test-year file.
# Calculate 2025 prevalence with that year's own survey weights.
scored <- load_run_rds("checkpoints", "07_scored_2025")
annual_test <- scored[
    valid_outcome(FMD) &
        valid_weight(RAW_WEIGHT) &
        cohort %in% primary_groups,
    .(
        observed_fmd = weighted_mean(FMD, RAW_WEIGHT),
        n = .N
    ),
    by = .(YEAR, cohort)
]

# Match column names and types explicitly before binding. Do not use
# fill = TRUE to silently create missing 2025 confidence intervals.
annual_test <- annual_test[, ..required_columns]
annual_all <- data.table::rbindlist(
    list(annual_history, annual_test),
    use.names = TRUE
)

data.table::setorder(annual_all, cohort, YEAR)
save_table(annual_all, "11_annual_fmd_2014_2025")
print(annual_all)

# A changing survey population may shift prevalence even without any causal effect.
trend_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(
    annual_all,
    ggplot2::aes(x = YEAR, y = observed_fmd, color = cohort)
) +
    ggplot2::geom_line() +
    ggplot2::geom_point() +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 2020, linetype = "dashed", color = atg_palette[["gold"]]) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2014:2025) +
    atg_scale_color_groups() +
    atg_theme() +
    ggplot2::labs(
        title = "Observed frequent mental distress across survey years",
        subtitle = "Annual survey-weighted rates; dashed marker at 2020 is descriptive",
        x = "Survey year",
        y = "Frequent mental distress prevalence",
        color = "Population",
        caption = "Repeated cross-sectional data; changing state coverage and population response may matter."
    )
show_and_save(trend_plot, "11_annual_fmd_2014_2025", 11, 6)
```


## Predictor distribution changes

Compares the weighted proportions in each predictor category across recent years; the visible example highlights income and its explicit `Missing` category. Variables may change because of survey participation or harmonization.

```{r predictor-shifts}
# Inspect only the late-development and subsequent evaluation years.
# The 2025 features are scored already; the source dataset is never modified.
historical <- read_historical()
historical <- historical[
    YEAR %in% c(2022L, 2023L, 2024L) & valid_weight(RAW_WEIGHT),
    .(
        YEAR, RAW_WEIGHT, FMD, AIAN_ALONE, PHYSHLTH_DAYS,
        GENHLTH_CLEAN, AGE_BAND, SEX_CLEAN, EDU_CLEAN, INCOME_BAND
    )
]
historical <- prepare_features(historical)
late_years <- data.table::rbindlist(list(
    historical[, c("YEAR", "RAW_WEIGHT", "FMD", "cohort", feature_names), with = FALSE],
    scored[, c("YEAR", "RAW_WEIGHT", "FMD", "cohort", feature_names), with = FALSE]
))
rm(historical)
gc(verbose = FALSE)

# Every estimate is weighted within its *own year*, not across pooled years.
# Weighted category shares can reveal drift in input distributions.
shift_rows <- list()
row_number <- 0L
for (variable in feature_names) {
    annual <- late_years[, .(
        weighted_total = sum(RAW_WEIGHT),
        respondents = .N
    ), by = .(YEAR, cohort, category = as.character(get(variable)))]
    annual[, weighted_share := weighted_total / sum(weighted_total), by = .(YEAR, cohort)]
    annual[, variable := variable]
    row_number <- row_number + 1L
    shift_rows[[row_number]] <- annual
}
shift_table <- data.table::rbindlist(shift_rows)
save_table(shift_table, "11_predictor_distributions_2022_2025")

# Focus the preview on income response categories and missingness.
income <- shift_table[
    variable == "INCOME_BAND" & cohort %in% primary_groups & YEAR %in% c(2023L, 2025L)
]
print(income[order(cohort, YEAR, category)])


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Compare income-category distributions, 2023 versus 2025
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Convert the existing long table into one row per
# population and income category, with a column for
# each survey year.

income_plot <- data.table::dcast(
    income,
    cohort + category ~ YEAR,
    value.var = "weighted_share"
)

# Give the annual share columns descriptive names.
data.table::setnames(
    income_plot,
    old = c("2023", "2025"),
    new = c("share_2023", "share_2025")
)

# Calculate the change in percentage points.
# Positive values indicate a larger share in 2025.
income_plot[
    ,
    change_pp := 100 * (share_2025 - share_2023)
]

# Validate that both survey years are represented.
stopifnot(
    !anyNA(income_plot$share_2023),
    !anyNA(income_plot$share_2025),
    all(is.finite(income_plot$change_pp))
)

# Order income categories logically rather than
# alphabetically. Reversed levels display the lowest
# income category at the top of a horizontal chart.
income_plot[
    ,
    category := factor(
        category,
        levels = rev(c(
            "<25k",
            "25-49k",
            "50-74k",
            "75k+",
            "Missing"
        ))
    )
]

# Ensure each group uses the same income categories.
stopifnot(!anyNA(income_plot$category))

# Save the exact comparison values.
save_table(
    income_plot,
    "11_income_distribution_change_2023_2025"
)

print(income_plot[order(cohort, category)])

# Provide room for numeric change annotations.
x_max <- max(
    income_plot$share_2023,
    income_plot$share_2025
) + 0.065

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Visualization: paired income-distribution estimates
# ------------------------------------------------------------

shift_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(
    income_plot,
    ggplot2::aes(y = category)
) +
    # Connect each category's 2023 and 2025 shares.
    ggplot2::geom_segment(
        ggplot2::aes(
            x = share_2023,
            xend = share_2025,
            yend = category
        ),
        color = atg_palette[["gold"]],
        linewidth = 1.2
    ) +
    # 2023 estimated share.
    ggplot2::geom_point(
        ggplot2::aes(
            x = share_2023,
            color = "2023"
        ),
        size = 3.5
    ) +
    # 2025 estimated share.
    ggplot2::geom_point(
        ggplot2::aes(
            x = share_2025,
            color = "2025"
        ),
        size = 3.5
    ) +
    # Show the exact percentage-point difference.
    ggplot2::geom_text(
        ggplot2::aes(
            x = pmax(share_2023, share_2025) + 0.015,
            label = sprintf("%+.1f pp", change_pp)
        ),
        hjust = 0,
        size = 3.3,
        color = atg_palette[["gold"]]
    ) +
    # Compare population groups in separate panels.
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(
        ~cohort,
        nrow = 1
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(
        values = c(
            "2023" = atg_year_colors[["2023"]],
            "2025" = atg_year_colors[["2025"]]
        )
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
        labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
        breaks = seq(0, 0.50, by = 0.10)
    ) +
    ggplot2::coord_cartesian(
        xlim = c(0, x_max)
    ) +
    atg_theme() +
    ggplot2::theme(
        legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(
            face = "bold",
            size = 11
        ),
        plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(
            size = 8,
            hjust = 0,
            margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 12)
        )
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(
        title = "How did income distributions shift between 2023 and 2025?",
        subtitle = paste(
            "Survey-weighted income-category shares",
            "by population"
        ),
        x = "Weighted respondent share",
        y = "Household income category",
        color = "Survey year",
        caption = paste(
            "Labels show the 2025 minus 2023 difference",
            "in percentage points.",
            "Income bands are nominal and include missing responses.",
            "\nDescriptive changes do not establish population trends",
            "or statistically significant differences."
        )
    )

show_and_save(
    shift_plot,
    "11_income_distribution_shift_dumbbell",
    12,
    6
)

```
```{r}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Visualize income distribution changes by population
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Positive values indicate a larger weighted share in 2025.
# Negative values indicate a smaller weighted share in 2025.
# These are descriptive differences, not significance tests.

shift_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(
    income_plot,
    ggplot2::aes(
        x = change_pp,
        y = category,
        color = cohort
    )
) +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(
        xintercept = 0,
        linetype = "dashed",
        color = atg_palette[["mauve"]],
        linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_segment(
        ggplot2::aes(
            x = 0,
            xend = change_pp,
            yend = category
        ),
        linewidth = 1.3
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
        size = 3.5
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_text(
        ggplot2::aes(
            x = change_pp + ifelse(change_pp >= 0, 0.2, -0.2),
            label = sprintf("%+.1f pp", change_pp),
            hjust = ifelse(change_pp >= 0, 0, 1)
        ),
        color = atg_palette[["gold"]],
        size = 3.5
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(
        ~cohort,
        nrow = 1
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
        labels = function(x) sprintf("%+g pp", x),
        expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 1)
    ) +
    atg_scale_color_groups() +
    atg_theme() +
    ggplot2::theme(
        legend.position = "none",
        strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(
            face = "bold"
        ),
        plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(
            size = 8,
            hjust = 0
        )
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(
        title = "How did income distributions shift from 2023 to 2025?",
        subtitle = "Change in survey-weighted income-category shares",
        x = "Change in weighted share (percentage points)",
        y = "Household income category",
        caption = paste(
            "Positive = larger share in 2025; negative = smaller share.",
            "\nDescriptive estimates only; income bands are not inflation-adjusted.",
            "Survey-design uncertainty is not shown."
        )
    )

show_and_save(
    shift_plot,
    "11_income_distribution_change",
    11,
    5.5
)

```
